2.1 Knowledge Distillation for Large Language Models

Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a widely adopted paradigm for transferring knowledge from high-capacity teacher models to smaller and less capable student models. For large language models (LLMs), KD is usually realized through two paradigms: sequence-level (text-based) distillation and logit-based (response-level) distillation.

Sequence-level knowledge distillation trains the student model using texts generated by the teacher as hard-label supervision, treating the teacher-produced outputs as pseudo-labels and optimizing the student via standard maximum-likelihood estimation (Kim and Rush, 2016). In contrast, besides the SFT loss based on ground-truth labels, logit-based KD additionally uses the teacher’s soft output distributions to distill fine-grained predictive information by aligning the teacher and student distributions. The pioneering logit-based KD method (Hinton et al., 2015) uses the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) to measure the discrepancy between the student and the teacher distributions. Reverse KLD (RKLD) employs a reverse version of KL divergence by changing the reference distribution in KL from the teacher to the student, allowing the student to concentrate its limited capacity on the teacher’s high-probability regions (Gu et al., 2024). AlphaNet (Wang et al., 2021) introduces α\alpha-divergence, providing a tunable measure between KLD and RKLD to penalize over-estimation and under-estimation in KD. ABKD (Wang et al., 2025) further proposes a novel α​-​β\alpha\text{-}\beta-divergence to balance hardness-concentration and confidence-concentration, generalizing FKLD and RKLD to a broader family of divergences.
2.2 Protecting LLMs from Knowledge Distillation

The great success of KD poses a significant threat to the protection of intellectual property in LLMs. To mitigate this issue, watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2026) seeks to embed an identifiable and verifiable signature into a model’s behavior or parameters, enabling the model owner to verify their ownership. Meanwhile, Fingerprinting (Ye et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2024) assigns a unique and traceable identity to each distributed model instance, enabling the model owner to attribute leaked or misused models to their source. Despite their usefulness, both approaches are inherently post hoc, indicating that they facilitate the identification of model stealing after it has occurred, but cannot prevent the extraction process itself.

Another research line attempts to directly solve this threat by modifying the token distribution during decoding to obtain generated texts that are resilient to distillation. The pioneering work (Savani et al., 2025) proposes an anti-distillation decoding strategy that actively poisons reasoning traces by injecting a learned perturbation into the token-level probability distribution. Concretely, a proxy student first computes gradients on a small hold-out set of teacher-generated sequences, yielding a fixed poisoning direction ∇ℓ\nabla\ell. During inference, the teacher performs two forward passes for each candidate token with proxy-student parameters perturbed by ±η∇ℓ\pm\eta\nabla\ell, and estimates the resulting finite-difference logit shift. This shift is then integrated into the teacher’s logits to form an adjusted sampling distribution. Sampling from this modified distribution implicitly steers any downstream student trained on these traces toward higher loss, thereby degrading the effectiveness of distillation. DOGe (Li et al., 2025) adopts a more direct approach that maximizes the divergence between teacher and student output distributions to make the teacher’s predictions harder to imitate. Specifically, DOGe fine-tunes the teacher’s final linear layer via the negative KL-divergence between the temperature-scaled softmax of the teacher logits and the detached softmax of a proxy student, enlarging the teacher–student discrepancy.

However, existing methods limit their scope in the sequence-level distillation scenarios, leaving the defense against the more widely discussed logit-based KD algorithms largely unexplored. To address this gap, this work makes an early step in investigating this issue from an information-theoretic perspective and proposes learning a transformation matrix as an effective post-processing solution.
3 Preliminary
3.1 Notation

Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be the vocabulary and |𝒱|<∞|\mathcal{V}|<\infty. Let X∈𝒱∗X\in\mathcal{V}^{*} be the input sequence consisting of the user’s query and the ongoing generated response, and Y∈𝒱Y\in\mathcal{V} be the ground-truth label, i.e., the next token for the current input XX.

Let f:𝒱∗→ℝ|𝒱|f:\mathcal{V}^{*}\to\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} be the large language model, and Z=f⁡(X)Z=f(X) be the logit vector for current input XX. The next token prediction is sampled from the distribution σ⁡(Z)\sigma(Z), where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) denotes the softmax function.
3.2 Knowledge Distillation

Given a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} consisting of prompt-answer pairs (q,o)(q,o), KD algorithms repeatedly query a teacher model fT​(⋅)f_{\text{T}}(\cdot) with (q,o)(q,o) sampled from 𝒟\mathcal{D} and train a student model fS​(⋅)f_{\text{S}}(\cdot) by mimicking the teacher’s output. Formally, the knowledge distillation loss can be expressed as:

ℒKD≜1l∑t=1lDist(σ(fT(q,o<t))∥σ(fS(q,o<t))),\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}}\triangleq\frac{1}{l}\sum_{t=1}^{l}\text{Dist}\Big(\sigma\big(f_{\text{T}}(q,o_{<t})\big)\Big\|\sigma\big(f_{\text{S}}(q,o_{<t})\big)\Big), (1)

where ll denotes the length of the ground-truth answer oo, and Dist(⋅∥⋅)\text{Dist}(\cdot\|\cdot) denotes the distance metric such as Kullback–Leibler divergence (KLD). In general, the objective of logit-based distillation algorithms can be formulated as:
ℒtotal=(1−α)⋅ℒSFT+α⋅ℒKD,\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=(1-\alpha)\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}+\alpha\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}}, (2)

where α\alpha is a factor set to 0.50.5 by default, and ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}} denotes the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) loss, i.e., the negative log-likelihood of the predictive probability of the ground-truth label. Since the logits convey more contextual information than the predictive label alone, KD typically outperforms standard SFT on many downstream tasks. Based on this formulation, various improved algorithms have been proposed, including novel designs of distance metrics such as reverse KLD (Gu et al., 2024) and AB-KLD (Wang et al., 2025).
3.3 Information Bottleneck

The Information Bottleneck (IB) theory (Tishby et al., 2000; Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015; Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby, 2017) highlights that a well-trained model should compress redundant information from inputs while preserving key information for tasks. The IB objective is formulated as:
ℒIB=ℐ⁡(X,Z)−β⋅ℐ⁡(Z,Y),\mathcal{L}_{\text{IB}}=\mathcal{I}(X;Z)-\beta\cdot\mathcal{I}(Z;Y), (3)

where ℐ⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathcal{I}(\cdot;\cdot) is mutual information, and β>0\beta>0 is a hyperparameter. A lower ℒIB\mathcal{L}_{\text{IB}} indicates a better performance and higher robustness of a model. Note that ZZ in IB represents the intermediate representation during inference. In this work, we instantiate ZZ as the logit vector.
4 Method

In this section, we first illustrate the rationality and benefits of minimizing CMI as a defense objective and present a theoretically-grounded post-processing strategy via a logit transformation matrix. Guided by theoretical insights, we design an optimization objective consisting of two complementary loss terms to train the matrix. An overview of the proposed method is illustrated in Figure 2.
4.1 Conditional Mutual Information-Based Defense

The CMI ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y) measures how much information ZZ reveals about XX given the ground-truth label YY. The additional contextual information that ZZ carries beyond the label aligns exactly with the goal of logit-based distillation, as shown in Equation 1. Therefore, we propose to defend teacher knowledge by minimizing ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y), preventing such contextual information from being extracted. This objective can also be interpreted through entropy and uncertainty. Specifically, ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)=ℋ⁡(X|Y)−ℋ⁡(X|Z,Y)\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y)=\mathcal{H}(X|Y)-\mathcal{H}(X|Z,Y), which quantifies the reduction in uncertainty of XX when ZZ is additionally observed. For a fixed training dataset, ℋ⁡(X|Y)\mathcal{H}(X|Y) remains constant. Hence, minimizing ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y) is equivalent to maximizing ℋ⁡(X|Z,Y)\mathcal{H}(X|Z,Y), i.e., making ZZ contain as little information about XX as possible to increase the uncertainty about XX given the label YY.

As an intuitive extreme case, if ZZ ideally degenerates to the one-hot label YY, i.e., it contains no contextual information beyond the category, then logit-based knowledge distillation collapses to standard label-only supervised fine-tuning. In this case, the CMI attains its minimum value ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)=ℐ⁡(X;Y|Y)=0\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y)=\mathcal{I}(X;Y|Y)=0.

To reduce the contextual information in teacher logits, we propose a lightweight post-processing strategy that further modifies output logits while keeping the teacher completely frozen. Concretely, we introduce a learnable matrix ℳ\mathcal{M} to transform the original teacher output into a refined one. Before delving into the full training pipeline, we show that such a transformation admits an intriguing information-theoretic property that formally guarantees that the refined logits become more context-compressed:

Let X∈𝒱∗X\in\mathcal{V}^{*} be the current input, Y∈𝒱Y\in\mathcal{V} be the ground-truth next token, Z=f⁡(X)∈ℝ|𝒱|Z=f(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} be the teacher logits, ℳ∈ℝ|𝒱|×|𝒱|\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times|\mathcal{V}|} be the logit transformation matrix, and Z′=ℳ⋅ZZ^{\prime}=\mathcal{M}\cdot Z be the refined logits. Then
Y→X→Z→Z′Y\to X\to Z\to Z^{\prime}
forms a Markov chain, and their CMI values satisfy
ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)≥ℐ⁡(X;Z′|Y).\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y)\geq\mathcal{I}(X;Z^{\prime}|Y).

Detailed proofs can be found in Appendix A. Theorem 2 ensures that matrix transformations are universally beneficial for reducing CMI, which facilitates the compression of contextual information exploited by attackers. To further reduce CMI while preserving the utility of outputs, we additionally design an effective optimization objective to better guide the training of the transformation matrix.
4.2 Transformation Matrix Optimization

Next, we analyze the proposed matrix training objective through the lens of the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle to resolve the optimization problem. In particular, the following property reveals that minimizing CMI actually induces an IB objective.
The conditional mutual information ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y) is a special case of Information Bottleneck objective with β=1\beta=1 in Equation 3, i.e.,
ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)=ℐ⁡(X,Z)−ℐ⁡(Z,Y).\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y)=\mathcal{I}(X;Z)-\mathcal{I}(Z;Y). (4)

A detailed derivation is provided in Appendix A. This property is particularly appealing as it reveals that minimizing ℐ⁡(X;Z|Y)\mathcal{I}(X;Z|Y) inherits the benefits of the Information Bottleneck, balancing compression of redundant information in XX while preserving task-relevant information in YY. The above characterization naturally decomposes the objective into two complementary sub-tasks:

Minimizing ℐ⁡(X,Z)\mathcal{I}(X;Z). This compresses redundant contextual information in the teacher logits ZZ that originates from the input XX, weakening the dependency between inputs and outputs. As a consequence, ZZ becomes less informative about XX, which enhances the resistance against KD algorithms.

Maximizing ℐ⁡(Z,Y)\mathcal{I}(Z;Y). This preserves task-relevant information and maintains the model’s utility. Notably, it encourages ZZ to concentrate toward its class centroid (i.e., increasing the correct label’s logit while suppressing others), which also eliminates contextual information and brings defense benefits.

Training Loss Design. Motivated by the two sub-tasks, we design two complementary loss functions to achieve the CMI minimization. We begin with analyzing the second term ℐ⁡(Z,Y)\mathcal{I}(Z;Y), which can be expanded into
ℐ⁡(Z,Y)=ℋ⁡(Y)−ℋ⁡(Y|Z).\mathcal{I}(Z;Y)=\mathcal{H}(Y)-\mathcal{H}(Y|Z). (5)

Note that ℋ⁡(Y)\mathcal{H}(Y) is constant, thus maximizing ℐ⁡(Z,Y)\mathcal{I}(Z;Y) is equivalent to minimizing the conditional entropy ℋ⁡(Y|Z)\mathcal{H}(Y|Z), which measures the residual uncertainty about the ground-truth label YY after observing logits ZZ. Although directly computing ℋ⁡(Y|Z)\mathcal{H}(Y|Z) is intractable, we can derive a consistent upper bound as follows.

Let Y∈𝒱Y\in\mathcal{V} be the ground-truth next token and Z∈ℝ|𝒱|Z\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} be the teacher logits. Let p(⋅|Z)p(\cdot|Z) be the distribution of YY conditional on ZZ, and p^(⋅|Z)=σ(Z)\hat{p}(\cdot|Z)=\sigma(Z) be its predictive distribution by the teacher model. Then the cross-entropy ℋ⁡(p,p^)\mathcal{H}(p,\hat{p}) can be decomposed into
ℋ(p,p^)=ℋ(Y|Z)+𝔼Z[𝕂𝕃(p(⋅|Z)∥p^(⋅|Z))],\mathcal{H}(p,\hat{p})=\mathcal{H}(Y|Z)+\mathbb{E}_{Z}\left[\mathbb{KL}\Big(p(\cdot|Z)\Big\|\hat{p}(\cdot|Z)\Big)\right], (6)
which further implies the upper bound
ℋ⁡(p,p^)≥ℋ⁡(Y|Z).\mathcal{H}(p,\hat{p})\geq\mathcal{H}(Y|Z). (7)

In classification tasks with discrete labels, p(⋅|Z)p(\cdot|Z) degenerates into a one-hot distribution, making ℋ⁡(p,p^)\mathcal{H}(p,\hat{p}) equivalent to the standard cross-entropy loss, denoted as ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}. Therefore, minimizing ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} provides a tractable surrogate for reducing the conditional entropy ℋ⁡(Y|Z)\mathcal{H}(Y|Z). In practice, optimizing ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} increases the logit corresponding to the true label. This intuitively aligns with the fact that if argmax​(Z)=Y\text{argmax}(Z)=Y always holds, the conditional entropy attains its minimum, ℋ⁡(Y|Z)=0\mathcal{H}(Y|Z)=0.

For maximizing ℐ⁡(X,Z)\mathcal{I}(X;Z), previous studies on image classification typically compute its value (Ye et al., 2024) or estimate it via variational upper bounds (Alemi et al., 2017). However, directly estimating ℐ⁡(X,Z)\mathcal{I}(X;Z) for autoregressive LLMs is fundamentally infeasible, since both XX and ZZ are in high-dimensional spaces, and their underlying distributions are difficult to approximate. To handle this challenge, we note that in KD scenarios, the information of XX residing in ZZ is ultimately exploited through how ZZ instructs the student’s output, which in practice materializes in the form of gradients that update the student’s parameters during training. Hence, the learning signals conveyed by the gradients serve as the effective carrier of the information of XX residing in ZZ, which motivates the following proposition:

Let θ\theta denote the parameters of a surrogate student model fS​(⋅)f_{\textnormal{S}}(\cdot). Under the standard KD setting, the information in ZZ about XX that can be exploited during distillation is operationally conveyed through the gradients of the loss with respect to θ\theta, i.e.,

𝒈\displaystyle\bm{g} =∇θ1l∑t=1l[−(1−α)⋅logσ(fS(q,o<t))ot\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\frac{1}{l}\sum_{t=1}^{l}\Big[-(1-\alpha)\cdot\log\sigma\big(f_{\textnormal{S}}(q,o_{<t})\big)_{o_{t}} (8) +α⋅𝕂𝕃(σ(fT(q,o<t))∥σ(fS(q,o<t)))].\displaystyle+\alpha\cdot\mathbb{KL}\Big(\sigma\big(f_{\textnormal{T}}(q,o_{<t})\big)\Big\|\sigma\big(f_{\textnormal{S}}(q,o_{<t})\big)\Big)\Big].

Based on the gradients 𝒈\bm{g}, we can characterize the information within teacher logits ZZ that is transmitted to the student during distillation. The optimization objective is accordingly reformulated as obtaining a transformed distribution Z′Z^{\prime} whose induced gradients 𝒈′\bm{g}^{\prime} contain as little valid information as possible. Since the original 𝒈\bm{g} represents the correct and informative update direction under KD, we aim to disrupt this signal by maximizing the angular deviation between 𝒈\bm{g} and 𝒈′\bm{g}^{\prime}, measured via cosine similarity. This strategy implicitly suppresses distillation-relevant information in ZZ through gradient distortion, significantly enhancing resistance to logit-based distillation attacks.
With the above loss terms, the training objective for learning the transformation matrix ℳ\mathcal{M} is formulated as:

\displaystyle ℒℳ=ℒCE+λ⋅ℒgrad,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{M}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}+\lambda\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}}, (9) =−1l∑t=1llogσ(fT(q,o<t))ot+λ⋅⟨𝒈,𝒈′⟩‖𝒈‖F​‖𝒈′‖F,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{l}\sum_{t=1}^{l}\log\sigma\big(f_{\textnormal{T}}(q,o_{<t})\big)_{o_{t}}+\lambda\cdot\frac{\langle\bm{g},\bm{g}^{\prime}\rangle}{\|\bm{g}\|_{F}\|\bm{g}^{\prime}\|_{F}},
where λ>0\lambda>0 is the scaling factor of ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grad}}, ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is the dot operation, and ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} denotes the Frobenius norm.

Transformation Matrix Optimization. The pseudocode of training algorithm is presented in Appendix C. Notably, a direct implementation of ℳ\mathcal{M} as a dense |𝒱|×|𝒱||\mathcal{V}|\times|\mathcal{V}| matrix is computationally prohibitive due to the large vocabulary size. To mitigate this, we parameterize ℳ\mathcal{M} via a low-rank decomposition ℳ=𝐄+𝐀𝐁\mathcal{M}=\mathbf{E}+\mathbf{AB}, where 𝐄\mathbf{E} denotes the identity matrix, and 𝐀∈ℝ|𝒱|×r\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times r} and 𝐁∈ℝr×|𝒱|\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times|\mathcal{V}|} are learnable matrices with decomposition rank rr. Moreover, directly computing full gradients renders the optimization of ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}} intractable due to their high dimensionality. To this end, we adopt the gradients of the student model’s second-to-last layer as a surrogate in the loss calculation, as they contain rich task-relevant information and closely align with the model’s predicting behaviors. Inspired by LoRA, we initialize 𝐀\mathbf{A} from 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) and initialize 𝐁=𝟎\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}, so that ℳ\mathcal{M} starts from 𝐄\mathbf{E} and ensures Z′=ZZ^{\prime}=Z at the beginning of training. This initialization yields more stable gradients and improves optimization effectiveness (Hu et al., 2022).
5 Experiments
5.1 Experimental Setup

Models and Datasets. Note that logit-based KD requires teachers and students to share the same tokenization to ensure one-to-one correspondence in token semantics. Hence, we select models from the same series to avoid engineering issues from vocabulary mismatches and better focus on defensive analysis. We consider two widely used LLM families, Qwen2.5 (Yang et al., 2024) and Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024). For the Qwen family, we use Qwen2.5-7B as the teacher model and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as the surrogate student. Distillation is performed on multiple student models with different scales and capacities, including Qwen2.5-3B/1.5B/0.5B. For the Llama family, we use Llama-3.1-8B as the teacher model and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as the surrogate student. The defensive performance is then evaluated on student models Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.2-1B.

Following prior work (Savani et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), we consider three widely used benchmarks, GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), and MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021). GSM8K is a math problem dataset with annotated reasoning chains; we use the standard split with 7,473 training and 1,319 evaluation examples. MMLU is a large-scale benchmark for evaluating world knowledge and problem-solving. We randomly sample 15,000 pairs as training data and evaluate on a test set of 14,042 examples. The MATH is a more challenging math benchmark, which contains 7,500 training examples with step-by-step solutions. Following (Xia et al., 2025), we evaluate performance on the MATH-500 (Lightman et al., 2023) dataset.

Distillation Baselines. We evaluate our method against four logit-based KD baselines that have exhibited competitive performance across a wide range of tasks: the classical logit-based KD (Hinton et al., 2015) with forward KLD, reverse KLD (RKLD) (Gu et al., 2024), AlphaNet (Wang et al., 2021), and the state-of-the-art ABKD (Wang et al., 2025).
Teacher Model GSM8K MMLU vanilla Ours vanilla Ours Qwen2.5-7B 80.89 79.83 73.85 72.84 Llama-3.1-8B 55.95 54.44 65.20 63.99

Implementation Details. We train the proposed transformation matrix for 5 epochs at a batch size of 32. For GSM8K and MATH, the learning rate is set to 5⋅10−75\cdot 10^{-7}, while for MMLU is 5⋅10−65\cdot 10^{-6}. The matrix decomposition rank is set to 32. The learning rate follows a linear warm-up schedule over the first 10% of total training steps and then decays to zero using cosine annealing. We optimize the matrix using AdamW with a weight decay of 0.01 and default momentum coefficients β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9 and β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999. We adopt the implementation and corresponding hyperparameter settings provided in (Wang et al., 2025), using α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and β=0.9\beta=0.9 for AlphaNet, and α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and β=0.8\beta=0.8 for ABKD. In Sec. 5.4, we explore the influence of the loss factor λ\lambda.
For a stable and reproducible evaluation, we conduct all experiments using greedy decoding. More details including student distillation configuration are in Appendix B.2.
5.2 Performance Evaluation

We first report the accuracy of defensive teacher models in Table 1. By maximizing the mutual information between Z′Z^{\prime} and YY using ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}, the learned matrix effectively preserves teacher accuracy. Figure 3 provides outputs generated from the original and the transformed teacher. As observed, our defensive teacher produces fluent and coherent responses while preserving task correctness. This contrasts with existing sequence-level distillation defenses that disrupt sampling distributions and induce texts with degraded quality.

We then present student distillation results in Table 2. The results show that the learned matrix strengthens distillation resistance and yields a consistent performance degradation on distilled students across different teacher–student pairs and datasets. E.g., distilling Qwen2.5-1.5B on GSM8K via AlphaNet incurs an accuracy drop of 11.98%, highlighting our effectiveness of suppressing distillation-relevant information. Notably, student models are jointly optimized using both the distillation loss ℒKD\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}} induced by teacher logits and an SFT loss computed from ground-truth labels. Our defense perturbs only the teacher logits and only affects ℒKD\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}, yet still misleads the distillation optimization and leads to a substantial degradation in student performance. Furthermore, we observe cases where distillation with the original logits surpasses its SFT-only counterpart, whereas using transformed logits performs even worse than SFT. This further validates that our strategy effectively suppresses the contextual information required for effective distillation.

We also observe that our defense has a stronger effect on GSM8K than MMLU, which we attribute to GSM8K’s longer multi-step mathematical reasoning, where perturbations accumulate along the reasoning trajectory and exert a more pronounced effect. By contrast, MMLU mainly involves multi-choice questions that LLMs typically resolve with a direct option selection, making it less sensitive to such disruptions. Due to space limits, we provide results on surrogate models in Appendix D and visualization of student outputs under distillation in Appendix E.

Loss Landscape. To reveal the underlying mechanism of our approach, we then analyze the training dynamics of the overall loss ℒℳ\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{M}} and the gradient deviation loss ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grad}}. As shown in Figure 5, the cosine similarity term ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}} starts around 11, indicating that the gradients of transformed logits are initialized to be identical to original ones (i.e., ℳ=𝐄\mathcal{M}=\mathbf{E} initially). In the first 300 steps, the overall loss ℒℳ\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{M}} decreases while ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}} remains nearly unchanged, implying that this stage mainly optimizes ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}. Afterwards, ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}} rapidly drops to negative values, indicating that the learned matrix induces a large gradient angular deviation.

Note that ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}} eventually stabilizes around −0.2-0.2, i.e., an angle of approximately 101.54∘101.54^{\circ}. This indicates that the transformed gradient direction becomes substantially misaligned with the original ones, reducing the distillation-relevant information and misleading the student’s updates.
5.3 Distillation on the MATH benchmark

Apart from the above two benchmarks, we further evaluate on the more challenging MATH benchmark, which contains significantly more difficult math problems. Since the Llama series performs poorly on this dataset, making the evaluation less informative, we conduct experiments using the stronger Qwen series.

Method Defense Qwen2.5 Series 3B 1.5B 0.5B SFT-Only – 49.40 31.80 20.80 KD vanilla 50.80 33.20 23.40 Ours 44.00 29.40 18.40 AlphaNet vanilla 51.80 33.20 23.60 Ours 43.60 29.00 17.00 MiniLLM vanilla 51.40 34.40 23.80 Ours 45.80 29.60 19.80 ABKD vanilla 52.60 34.00 25.80 Ours 46.60 29.40 18.80

After applying the learned matrix, the teacher’s accuracy decreases only marginally from 53.8% to 50.4%. In contrast, Table 3 shows that distilled students suffer a far more pronounced degradation. E.g., under KD with Qwen2.5-3B, the accuracy drops by a notable value of 6.8%. This again confirms the effectiveness and universality of our CMI-inspired defense across different datasets.
5.4 Ablation Study
We conduct ablation analysis on Qwen using GSM8K under standard KD. More ablations are in Appendix D.

Ablation on the matrix loss parameter λ\lambda. λ\lambda is the scaling factor that balances the contributions of ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} and ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}} during matrix training in Eq. (9). The left subfigure of Figure 5 shows that when increasing λ\lambda, there is a general trend of decreasing student accuracy, which confirms that ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\text{grad}} further reduces distillation-relevant information. However, overly large λ\lambda also leads to a noticeable drop in the teacher’s accuracy. We then choose λ=1\lambda=1 to achieve a better trade-off between defense strength and utility preservation.

Ablation on the decomposition rank rr of ℳ\mathcal{M}. The right subfigure of Figure 5 reveals a trade-off between teacher utility and defensive efficacy. When the rank rr is small, the limited capacity mainly prioritizes minimizing ℒCE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}, preserving teacher accuracy but insufficient defensive effects. In contrast, larger rr allows more capacity for optimizing ℒgrad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grad}}, enhancing defense while potentially compromising teacher accuracy. To balance defense effectiveness and model utility, we adopt r=32r=32 as the default setting.
6 Conclusion

In this paper, we investigate the challenging problem of defending LLMs against unauthorized logit-based KD. We characterize the guidance signals in the teacher logits via conditional mutual information, based on which we propose a post-processing approach that learns a transformation matrix using two theory-inspired loss functions. By refining the output logits, the proposed method degrades the performance of distilled student models while preserving teacher utility, effectively protecting the intellectual property. We highlight that, unlike prior defenses against sequence-level distillation, our method makes a pioneering step in defending against tricky logit-based KD techniques. We hope this work advances the community’s understanding of LLM distillation and motivates more robust distillation defenses.

core.text: 2 Related Work
2.1 Preference-based Post-training

Building on base LLMs, recent research has explored various strategies to bolster agentic capabilities. For instance, Li et al. (2025b) integrates a Deep Web Explorer into a think-search-draft loop, utilizing DPO with human feedback for complex report generation. Similarly, Wu et al. (2025b) constructs localized preference pairs from debugging traces to apply targeted preference optimization. Our approach is most closely related to Goldie et al. (2025), which synthesizes step-wise reasoning data and employs preference-based RL to fine-tune the model. Related to our step-level preference construction, AlphaLLM-CPL (Wang et al., 2024) distills MCTS search into stepwise trajectory preference pairs and applies curriculum preference learning to emphasize key learning steps. We extend this framework to agent domains by introducing a method to identify critical steps, thereby improving computational efficiency and reducing complexity.
2.2 Entropy-enhanced Algorithms for RL

Recent findings in RLVR, particularly Wang et al. (2025c), demonstrate that only a small fraction of high-entropy tokens fundamentally drive effective reinforcement learning for reasoning tasks. Similarly, Cheng et al. (2025) also found that assigning advantages in accordance with entropy leads to better reasoning performances. In terms of the long-horizon agent domain, Wang et al. (2025a); Xu et al. (2025) further proposed entropy-based algorithms to enhance agents’ training. This suggests that selective supervision on entropy, which corresponds to critical decision points, may be more effective than uniform or dense supervision. Inspired by this principle, our work identifies critical branching points in agent trajectories and applies verified, fine-grained supervision selectively at these pivotal decisions, combining the reliability of outcome-based verification with the precision of step-level supervision.
3 Methodology

We formalize the agentic decision-making process as ReAct trajectories (§3.1) and introduce our Critical Step Optimization (CSO) framework. Our key idea is to identify verified critical steps in failed policy trajectories where alternative actions can flip task outcomes, and construct fine-grained preference pairs from these verified critical steps for targeted DPO training (§3.2). This process can be applied iteratively to progressively refine the policy (§3.3). Figure 2 illustrates the complete CSO pipeline.

3.2 Verified Critical Step Collection

Unlike trajectory-level DPO that contrasts entire successful and failed trajectories, or step-level methods that provide estimated but often inaccurate rewards at every step, our approach focuses on verified critical steps, meaning steps where taking an alternative action can demonstrably flip the task outcome from failure to success.

4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Settings
Policy Model and Framework

We use CK-Pro-8B (Fang et al., 2025) as our policy model, an 8B-parameter agent model obtained by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) base model. All agent interactions are executed through the Cognitive Kernel Pro framework, which is a fully open-source and free multi-module agent framework. It features a main agent responsible for orchestrating specialized sub-agents dedicated to web navigation, file handling, and tool invocation, providing a standardized and extensible environment for agent usage. We extend the Cognitive Kernel Pro framework to support two critical features for our experiments: (1) execution of Process Reward Model (PRM) scoring directly within agent steps, and (2) seamless continuation of agent rollouts from any given intermediate state. We leverage the LlamaFactory (Zheng et al., 2024) framework for all post-training.
Training Data and Expert Model

Our DPO preference data is constructed starting from the SFT training data of CK-Pro-8B, which contains 47K task-trajectory pairs covering diverse reasoning and tool-use scenarios. We deploy the policy model on these tasks to collect failed trajectories, then use Claude-3.7-Sonnet as the expert model to generate high-quality alternative actions.
Hyperparameters

For DPO training, we set the KL penalty coefficient β=0.5\beta=0.5. For critical step identification, we sample K=5K=5 alternative candidates at each potential branching point. We conduct iterative training for up to 2 rounds, where each round collects fresh failed trajectories from the updated policy. PRM scoring uses Claude-3.7-Sonnet with rubric-based evaluation (see Appendix A). For PRM thresholds, we set γhigh=0.65\gamma_{\text{high}}=0.65 and γlow=0.45\gamma_{\text{low}}=0.45 to identify candidate critical steps. All experimental results are reported based on three independent runs to mitigate variability due to network conditions and external factors. As web search is involved in several tasks, some results may exhibit minor differences from the original papers.
4.2 Benchmarks and Baselines
Benchmarks

We evaluate on two challenging agent benchmarks: GAIA-Text-103 (Mialon et al., 2023): As our model is text-only, we follow WebThinker (Li et al., 2025b) and report the text-only subset of the GAIA benchmark. This subset contains 103 questions spanning three difficulty levels (L1, L2, L3) requiring multi-step reasoning and tool orchestration. We report this subset as our models are pure text-based agents. XBench-DeepSearch (Chen et al., 2025): A complex information retrieval and reasoning benchmark requiring deep search strategies and evidence synthesis across multiple web sources. We choose 2505 version which contains 100 complex tasks. For all benchmarks, we follow the evaluation protocol of WebThinker and CK-Pro-8B, using an LLM to determine whether each output is correct, referencing the gold answer as ground truth.

Baselines

We compare against several categories of methods: Proprietary Models: GPT-4.1 and Claude-3.7-Sonnet as strong closed-source baselines. Open-Source Models: Qwen3-8B (base model) and CK-Pro-8B (SFT baseline). Post-Training Methods: We implement several post-training baselines within the Cognitive Kernel Pro framework to ensure fair comparison. Exploration-based Trajectory Optimization (ETO) (Song et al., 2024) constructs preference pairs by using expert-generated successful trajectories as positive examples and policy-generated failed trajectories as negative examples, applying trajectory-level DPO. Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT) (Zhang et al., 2025) collects successful trajectories generated by the policy model itself and performs supervised fine-tuning on these successful cases. Step-wise DPO (Choudhury, 2025) applies dense step-level preference learning at every step in trajectories using PRM scoring; notably, we use the same PRM implementation (Claude-3.7-Sonnet with rubric-based evaluation) as our method to control for PRM quality. Iterative Process Refinement (IPR) (Xiong et al., 2024) constructs step-level rewards by identifying steps in outcome-verified successful trajectories as positive examples and corresponding steps in failed policy trajectories as negative examples, applying step-level DPO with these outcome-grounded signals.
4.3 Main Results
CSO achieves strong performance matching proprietary models.

Table 1 presents the performance comparison across all methods. Our Critical Step Optimization achieves 49.5% overall accuracy on GAIA-Text-103, a 37% relative improvement over the SFT baseline. Notably, CSO enables the open-source 8B model CK-Pro-8B to match the performance of GPT-4.1. CSO achieves consistent gains across all difficulty levels and substantially outperforms all post-training baselines by at least +5.0 points on both GAIA and XBench-DeepSearch.
Trajectory-level methods show limited effectiveness.

RFT shows no significant change (34.9%) by training on the policy’s own successful trajectories. ETO performs better (38.9%, +3.0 points) by contrasting expert successes against policy failures. Both methods suffer from coarse credit assignment by applying outcome-based rewards uniformly across all steps.
Step-level and hybrid methods face accuracy and noise issues.

Step-DPO achieves strong performance on simple L1 tasks (+7.1 points) but shows no improvement on harder L2/L3 tasks, revealing PRM accuracy degradation on complex reasoning. IPR improves through outcome verification (44.6% overall) but still suffers from outcome reward contamination. In contrast, CSO achieves +5.0 points over IPR by focusing exclusively on verified critical steps with precise credit assignment.
5 Analysis
5.1 CSO Ablations
Expert Positive Examples with Policy Negative Examples Achieve Best Performance.

To understand what types of preference pairs contribute most to learning, we systematically compare three data source configurations: (1) expert successes with expert failures, (2) policy successes with policy failures, and (3) expert successes with policy failures. All configurations start from the same failed policy trajectories and identify the same critical steps, differing only in the source of positive and negative actions. As shown in Table 2, combining expert successes with policy failures achieves the best performance, substantially outperforming both expert-only and policy-only pairs. This suggests that the most effective learning signal comes from contrasting expert demonstrations with the policy’s own failure modes at critical junctures, enabling the model to learn from high-quality behaviors while recognizing its specific weaknesses.

5.2 Impact of PRM Quality and Usage

We analyze how PRM quality and usage affect final performance. Specifically, we compare two PRM sources (Claude-3.7-Sonnet and GPT-4.1) and two usage paradigms: (1) CSO, which leverages the PRM for candidate selection combined with outcome verification, and (2) step-level Best-of-N (BoN), which uses PRM to directly select actions from sampled candidates. All experiments are conducted on CK-Pro-8B and evaluated on GAIA-Text-103-L1. In both settings, the number of candidates kk per step is fixed at 5 to ensure a controlled comparison.

The results indicate two key observations. First, the strength of the underlying foundation model is critical for PRM quality: Claude-3.7-Sonnet consistently yields higher performance than GPT-4.1 as a PRM, suggesting that models with stronger downstream task performance produce more reliable process rewards. Second, the CSO paradigm integrating PRM selection with explicit outcome verification achieves superior results relative to PRM-guided search alone. Notably, for the same PRM, CSO markedly outperforms step-BoN, highlighting CSO’s ability to mitigate PRM noise through outcome-based validation, whereas BoN is fully dependent on potentially noisy PRM-driven judgments. These findings validate our approach of using the PRM primarily for efficient candidate identification, subsequently filtered by robust outcome verification, rather than as a direct arbiter for action selection.
5.3 Analysis On Iterative Online Refinement

We compare CSO against ETO (Song et al., 2024) and IPR (Xiong et al., 2024) across four online training rounds on CK-Pro-8B, evaluated on GAIA-Text-103-L1. As shown in Figure 3, the three methods exhibit distinctly different behaviors. ETO initially improves but then degrades significantly, falling below the SFT baseline by Round 3 due to trajectory-level supervision uniformly penalizing all steps in failed trajectories, causing the policy to unlearn correct behaviors. IPR achieves more stable improvement, reaching 56.4% at Round 2-3, benefiting from Monte Carlo step-level rewards. However, IPR still propagates trajectory-level outcome signals to all steps, limiting further gains. In contrast, CSO achieves 61.5% by Round 2 and maintains this through Round 3, consistently outperforming both baselines. By focusing exclusively on verified critical steps, CSO avoids credit assignment noise and enables more effective online improvement.
5.4 Categorizing Critical Steps

We manually analyze a subset of PRM-identified critical steps and categorize them by error type. As shown in Figure 4, the identified critical steps distribute across several categories: Tool Invocation errors (26.1%) represent the largest category, including incorrect tool selection or suboptimal query formulation for search and retrieval operations. Reasoning Errors (25.1%) involve logical mistakes or incorrect calculations during task execution. Other Errors (24.1%) include miscellaneous issues such as parsing errors or edge case handling. Task Understanding errors (13.0%) stem from misinterpreting task requirements, while Information Extraction errors (11.7%) occur when the agent locates relevant information but fails to extract it correctly. This distribution demonstrates that CSO effectively identifies diverse types of critical decision points where the policy makes pivotal errors, validating that our method targets semantically meaningful steps rather than arbitrary positions in trajectories.
6 Conclusion

We introduced Critical Step Optimization (CSO), a post-training approach that focuses preference learning on verified critical steps where alternative actions demonstrably flip task outcomes. Inspired by findings that only high-entropy tokens drive effective RL for reasoning, we demonstrate that agent trajectories similarly contain a sparse subset of critical steps that determine success. Our method combines PRM selection with outcome verification to construct fine-grained preference data without trajectory-level coarseness or step-level estimation noise. Experiments show that CSO achieves 37% and 26% relative improvements over SFT on GAIA-Text-103 and XBench-DeepSearch, enabling an open-source 8B model to match GPT-4.1 while requiring supervision at only 16% of steps. CSO substantially outperforms trajectory-level, dense step-level, and hybrid methods, demonstrating that selective verified supervision provides an efficient framework for agent post-training.

core.text: 2 Related Work

Mitigating hallucinations necessitates a delicate balance between maximizing response correctness and ensuring effective refusal of unanswerable queries. Refusal-Aware Instruction Tuning (RAIT) explicitly trains models to generate specific refusal indicators for unknown questions, such as outputting ”I don’t know” (Cheng et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024) or appending uncertainty markers (Zhang et al., 2024a). Although advanced methods like CRaFT (Zhu et al., 2025) attempt to alleviate over-refusal by concurrently fine-tuning on high-certainty and unsolvable samples, these supervised approaches may inadvertently constrain general reasoning capabilities. Confidence-based strategies leverage model uncertainty to determine abstention decisions at inference time (Jurayj et al., 2025). Implementing these strategies effectively necessitates precise calibration techniques (Sun et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Damani et al., 2025), and the reliance on fixed thresholds can be sensitive to specific task distributions, potentially affecting generalization. Recently, RLVR methods have explored incentivizing refusal by penalizing hallucinations through multi-dimensional (Chen et al., 2025a) or multi-level rewards (Wei et al., 2025); nevertheless, such coarse-grained outcome rewards might provide limited guidance for optimizing the fine-grained intermediate reasoning process.

In multi-hop QA, LLMs optimized via outcome-driven RL often generate reasoning chains that are irrelevant to the target objective. Existing literature frequently attributes this faithfulness issue primarily to factual errors (Huang et al., 2025a; Agarwal et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025c). To address this, prevalent verification methods decompose responses into independent atomic claims for retrieval-based fact-checking, as exemplified by HalluMeasure (Akbar et al., 2024), KnowHalu (Zhang et al., 2024b), and others (Paul et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Li and Ng, 2025). While effective at mitigating hallucinations arising from factual inaccuracies, these claim-centric strategies may be less effective in addressing invalid logical processes.

4 Methodology
In this section, we introduce the FaithRL framework in detail, with the overall process illustrated in Figure 2.
4.1 Optimization Objectives

We assess model performance by partitioning the trajectory space 𝒯\mathcal{T} into three distinct outcomes. The correct set Sc={τ∈𝒯∣ψ⁡(τ)=A∗}S_{c}=\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}\mid\psi(\tau)=A^{*}\} includes trajectories where the model provides the correct answer or properly refuses an unanswerable query. The miss set Sm={τ∈𝒯∣ψ⁡(τ)=IDK∧A∗≠IDK}S_{m}=\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}\mid\psi(\tau)=\text{IDK}\land A^{*}\neq\text{IDK}\} represents false refusals, occurring only when the model incorrectly declines to answer a valid question. All other errors fall into the hallucination Set Sh={τ∈𝒯∣ψ⁡(τ)∈ℋ}S_{h}=\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}\mid\psi(\tau)\in\mathcal{H}\}. We denote the probabilities of these outcomes for a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} as correctness P⁡(C)P(C), miss rate P⁡(M)P(M), and hallucination rate P⁡(H)P(H).
Conventional optimization paradigms in QA typically prioritize one of the following objectives:
Objective A (maximize correctness): Maximize P⁡(C)P(C). This is the standard objective for general QA (Li et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a).
Objective B (minimize hallucination): Minimize P⁡(H)P(H). This is often prioritized in safety-critical applications (Liu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024).

In contrast, we propose objective C (maximize reasoning faithfulness). This objective targets the reasoning-faithful set Sf={τ∈𝒯∣ϕ⁡(τ)=ℰ⁡(q)}S_{f}=\{\tau\in\mathcal{T}\mid\phi(\tau)=\mathcal{E}(q)\}, which consists of trajectories where the used knowledge strictly matches the required evidence. Our goal is to maximize P⁡(F)=P⁡(τ∈Sf)P(F)=P(\tau\in S_{f}). Based on Assumptions 3.3 and 3.4, this objective naturally unifies accuracy and honesty because strict adherence to evidence guarantees the correct answer while precluding hallucination. This formulation ensures that every step in the reasoning chain makes a necessary contribution to the deduction, rather than merely supporting a correct final guess.
The following theorem demonstrates that while standard objectives push models toward extreme behaviors, optimizing for reasoning faithfulness aligns refusal decisions with model capability.
Consider a model with imperfect intrinsic capability. Optimizing the three defined objectives leads to distinct asymptotic behaviors for the miss rate P⁡(M)P(M):
Objective A (maximize correctness) forces P⁡(M)→0P(M)\to 0. This results in over-confidence, where the model speculates on all queries to maximize rewards.
Objective B (minimize hallucination) drives P⁡(M)→1P(M)\to 1. This leads to over-conservativeness, causing the model to refuse answerable queries to avoid hallucination risks.

Objective C (maximize reasoning faithfulness) ensures stability. It maintains the miss rate at a stable equilibrium determined by the model’s intrinsic capability, effectively preventing the degenerate collapse observed in objectives A and B.

4.2 Faithfulness-aware Reinforcement Learning

We propose FaithRL, a RL framework designed to maximize the faithfulness objective P⁡(F)P(F). To achieve this, FaithRL integrates a geometric reward mechanism that aligns outcome-level optimization with the model’s intrinsic capability, and a faithfulness-aware advantage modulation strategy that enforces step-level process supervision.
4.2.1 Geometric Reward Design

Existing strategies for optimizing reasoning tasks often rely on independent metrics for correctness and hallucination, which may fail to accurately quantify the genuine performance gain after optimization. To simultaneously address helpfulness and honesty without relying on arbitrary hyperparameters, we adopt the truthful helpfulness score (THS) (Zhu et al., 2025) as a higher-order metric that provides a geometrically intuitive fusion of utility and honesty.

As seen in Figure 3, we represent the model’s capability as a point on a two-dimensional plane, where the x-axis denotes the correctness rate and the y-axis represents the hallucination rate. Let E0=(x0,y0)E_{0}=(x_{0},y_{0}) be the initial capability point corresponding to the baseline, E1E_{1} be the point after optimization, and OO be the origin. The ideal strategy E∗​(1,0)E^{*}(1,0) denotes 100% correctness with zero hallucinations. THS is defined as the normalized signed area:

This metric effectively captures the degree of model refinement. Crucially, maximizing this signed area aligns perfectly with the dual goals of increasing correctness and reducing hallucinations, providing a robust measure of optimization quality. 4.2.2 Faithfulness-Aware Advantage Modulation

Geometric rewards optimize the final outcome, but they treat the reasoning process as a black box. To ensure faithfulness, we must verify that every single step contributes validly to the result. This requires supervision at the process level. We introduce faithfulness-aware advantage modulation (FAAM) to strictly enforce this step-wise fidelity.

Adopting the structure from Section 3.1, we decompose the trajectory τ\tau into discrete reasoning steps (s1,…,sk)(s_{1},\dots,s_{k}) and a final answer. 5 Experiments
5.1 Experimental Setup

We conduct evaluations on three multi-hop reasoning benchmarks: 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020), HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), and MuSiQue-Full (Trivedi et al., 2022). MuSiQue-Full naturally includes a mix of answerable and unanswerable questions. In contrast, the 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA datasets only contain answerable queries. To bridge this gap, we synthesize unanswerable samples for them, resulting in the 2WikiMultiHopQA-Full and HotpotQA-Full datasets. Specifically, for each question qq, we remove exactly one evidence document from 𝒦⁡(q)\mathcal{K}(q), which is the set of discrete documents. This manipulation ensures that the reasoning chain is logically broken, while the remaining knowledge retains high semantic relevance to qq. This design strictly compels the model to determine answerability through genuine reasoning, effectively preventing it from exploiting superficial heuristics (e.g., keyword matching) or reward hacking to shortcut the judgment process. We strictly filter these samples to ensure validity (see Appendix G.1). We train our model on the MuSiQue-Full dataset and evaluate performance on the test sets of all three full benchmarks.

We adopt THS as our primary evaluation metric, as defined in Section 4.2. Additionally, we report the correctness rate P⁡(C)P(C) and hallucination rate P⁡(H)P(H) to provide a complete performance profile.

We evaluate FaithRL against four categories of strong baselines: (1) refusal-aware SFT: We select R-Tuning (Zhang et al., 2024a) and CRaFT (Zhu et al., 2025). These methods explicitly incorporate refusal data into instruction tuning to teach the model when to abstain. (2) confidence-based abstention: We apply the CTSF thresholding strategy (Jurayj et al., 2025) to three distinct models: the original backbone, a GRPO-optimized model, and an RLCR-calibrated model (Damani et al., 2025). (3) RLVR methods: We include GRPO and TruthRL (Wei et al., 2025). These approaches optimize outcomes using sparse rewards, focusing on maximizing correctness and penalizing hallucinations. (4) factuality-driven RL: We evaluate FSPO (Li and Ng, 2025) and KnowRL (Ren et al., 2025). These methods utilize factuality-centric rewards to guide the reasoning process.
5.2 Main Results
Table 1 shows the overall experimental results, providing a comprehensive comparison between FaithRL and various baselines.

FaithRL consistently demonstrates superior performance in terms of THS across all settings. Compared with RLVR methods, FaithRL achieves an average improvement of +9.0 points on the in-domain MuSiQue-Full dataset and +18.5 points on the other two QA datasets. Specifically, FaithRL achieves a remarkable THS of 64.2% using the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct backbone, outperforming the strongest baseline, TruthRL (54.4%), by a margin of 9.8 points. This advantage is particularly pronounced on HotpotQA-Full, where FaithRL leads the next best methods by absolute margins of 13.6 and 9.3 points on the Llama and Qwen backbones, respectively. These outcomes empirically support the efficacy of our geometric reward design in achieving an optimal equilibrium between helpfulness and honesty.

Beyond the aggregate THS metric, FaithRL achieves the highest average correctness while simultaneously maintaining the lowest hallucination rate. Compared with other RLVR methods, FaithRL achieves an average correctness improvement of 1.6 points and a hallucination reduction of 4.7 points. For instance, averaging across Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct tasks, FaithRL records 84.3% correctness and a 9.8% hallucination rate, surpassing GRPO with a 3.6% increase in accuracy and a 6.3% reduction in hallucinations. This Pareto optimality powerfully demonstrates that our method does not merely seek a trade-off between utility and honesty, but rather achieves a fundamental elevation in intrinsic model capability driven by faithful reasoning.

The performance of baseline methods reveals distinct characteristics. While refusal-aware SFT (e.g., CRaFT) and confidence-based abstention (e.g., CTSF) effectively curtail hallucinations compared to prompting baselines, they fail to yield significant gains in correctness. Conversely, RL methods like TruthRL and KnowRL enhance performance on the in-domain MuSiQue-Full dataset but exhibit diminished gains on other QA benchmarks. For example, using the Llama model, TruthRL experiences a THS drop of 11.7 and 19.8 points on 2WikiMultihopQA-Full and HotpotQA-Full respectively compared to in-domain performance. In contrast, FaithRL maintains stability with a negligible drop of 2.6 points. This highlights the robust generalization capabilities of FaithRL across diverse reasoning tasks. 5.3 FaithRL Enhances Reasoning Faithfulness

We first investigate the ability of FaithRL to dynamically refine reasoning patterns throughout the optimization process. In this experiment, we train the Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct model on the MuSiQue-Full dataset with 15,000 samples. For every training step, we monitor the reasoning trajectories of each sample and calculate the faithful step ratio, defined as the proportion of reasoning steps strictly supported by evidence relative to the total steps. As illustrated in Figure 4, our analysis reveals that FaithRL stands out as the only method capable of driving a significant and sustained increase in reasoning faithfulness. Specifically, the overall ratio of faithful steps increased from an initial baseline of 51.4% to 82.5% after training. In contrast, standard RL baselines, including GRPO and TruthRL, did not show meaningful improvements in faithfulness ratios. This disparity highlights the fundamental advantage of our approach. Unlike traditional outcome-oriented optimization, FaithRL provides precise step-level guidance to effectively shape the underlying reasoning process of the model. We also provide a comprehensive breakdown of the training dynamics, categorized by sample correctness and step faithfulness, in Appendix H.2.

To demonstrate that the faithfulness learned by FaithRL is a robust cognitive capability rather than a dataset-specific artifact, we evaluate the models on two Out-of-Distribution (OOD) benchmarks, GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MATH500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), comparing FaithRL against the GRPO baseline. To obtain faithfulness metrics, we employ an LLM to perform sentence-wise comparisons against the ground-truth solution processes. These evaluations are strictly inference-only, ensuring that no answer leakage or training signals are provided. Details regarding the experimental setup are provided in Appendix G.3.

As shown in Figure 5, FaithRL consistently outperforms GRPO. In terms of performance, FaithRL achieves significantly higher accuracy, surpassing GRPO by 14.6% on GSM8k, while simultaneously maintaining a substantially lower hallucination rate. Regarding faithfulness, FaithRL exhibits a marked improvement in the overall faithful step ratio. Breakdown analysis shows this increase is primarily driven by improved faithfulness within correctly answered samples (rising from 52.3% to 68.3% on GSM8k). This suggests that the performance gains stem from genuine reasoning improvements rather than lucky guesses. We provide detailed results in Appendix H.3.

6 Conclusion

We presented FaithRL, a novel RL framework that enhances reasoning faithfulness by step-level verification. By strictly aligning model incentives with the validity of the reasoning process, our approach effectively bridges the gap between capability and honesty. Our extensive experiments confirm that FaithRL not only achieves superior performance in terms of correctness and hallucination reduction but also successfully internalizes faithful reasoning patterns.
